_about: Every attack SynQt claims to defend, and the test that proves it still fails.
This is an index, not a suite. Each of these tests lives beside the code it is about,
because that is where somebody changing that code will run it; what this file adds is
the other half, which no scattered set of tests can give on its own: a list of the
attack surface that can be read in one sitting, and a guard that fails when an entry
names a test that is no longer there. tools/synqt/tests/test_security_index.py is that
guard, and it runs in the ordinary pytest job on all three platforms.
The rule for adding one: a defect found by review or by report gets a test that fails
without the fix, and an entry here. Proving the test catches the bug is done by reverting
the fix and watching it go red; the entry is what stops that proof from being a thing

attacks.what: A page on another origin opens a WebSocket to the edge, and the browser attaches the victim's session cookie to it.
attacks.defended_by: The upgrade verifier compares Origin against security.allowed_origins before a socket exists. A browser cannot forge Origin.

attacks.what: A hand-written client presents a session cookie it made up, or none at all.
attacks.defended_by: The verifier looks the credential up in the session manager and denies 401 before a socket exists.

attacks.what: A visitor signs out, and the tab that was open keeps receiving everything the owner pushes to the connect points that session had acquired.
attacks.defended_by: Ending a session closes the connections it authorized. Which points a connection hosts is decided once, at the upgrade, so revoking the credential has to take the socket with it.

attacks.what: Session.logout() resets the client and leaves the session alive at the edge, so the next page load signs the visitor straight back in.
attacks.defended_by: SynClient answers the request by reaching the edge's logout route; the session is gone from the edge afterwards.

attacks.what: A caller with no identity connects to an edge whose project requires one.
attacks.defended_by: The verifier refuses it at the upgrade, before any object exists.

attacks.what: A signed-in user calls a slot their scope does not permit, or asks for another user's rows.
attacks.defended_by: The owner authorizes Caller inside every privileged slot; a consumer-side check is never the boundary.

attacks.what: A process on the network dials a mesh listener with no client certificate.
attacks.defended_by: Both ends verify the peer against the project CA; the handshake fails before any connection exists.

attacks.what: The same, with a certificate from some other authority.
attacks.defended_by: The CA is the project's own and is the only one either end trusts.

attacks.what: An entity holding a valid project certificate acquires a connect point it was never listed as a consumer of.
attacks.defended_by: Deny by default: the owner refuses a connection from an entity the point does not name, certificate or no certificate.

attacks.what: Anything but the web edge calls the database's connect point.
attacks.defended_by: The database authorizes the calling entity by its verified certificate subject inside the slot.

attacks.what: A consumer calls setData on a replicated model and the owner's rows change under it.
attacks.defended_by: SynQt::SourceModel refuses a write that arrived from a replica; a consumer that wants owner state changed calls a slot.

attacks.what: A consumer calls setData on the model its facade handed it. The write never reaches the owner, but QtRO's model Replica takes it into its own cache and answers true, so that consumer goes on showing a value nobody else has.
attacks.defended_by: The facade hands out SynQt::ReadOnlyModel over the Replica's model, never the Replica's own: setData returns false and flags() clears ItemIsEditable, so a delegate offers no editor and a direct caller is refused. The owner-side half is SynQt::SourceModel.

attacks.what: A row carries a field the contract never declared (an owner id, an email) and it reaches the browser.
attacks.defended_by: The boundary keeps the declared roles and drops the rest, where the rows are published.

attacks.what: A value longer than the contract's declared width is published or passed, and the receiver stores whatever arrives.
attacks.defended_by: A declared width is a rule the owner keeps at the boundary: the publish is refused whole rather than truncated into something that looks right.

attacks.what: The same, on the way out, where nothing on the receiving side would ever see the original.
attacks.defended_by: The signal is not raised at all.

attacks.what: A caller-supplied value carries SQL and the statement runs it.
attacks.defended_by: Every value is bound, never concatenated; the payload is stored and read back as the text it is.

attacks.what: A URL that is not the declared place but begins with its text (userinfo, a host suffix, a path suffix) is called, and the endpoint's declared headers, which is where the API key lives, go with it.
attacks.defended_by: The allowlist compares scheme, host, port and path segments, and refuses userinfo outright.

attacks.what: A release build reaches a database or an upstream API over an unverified plaintext connection.
attacks.defended_by: Refused in release, on both the provider and the outbound HTTP path.

attacks.what: An attacker hands a victim a valid state and their own authorization code, so the victim ends up signed in as the attacker.
attacks.defended_by: The callback must carry the state cookie the login set in that same browser, compared in constant time.

attacks.what: A callback arrives with a state this edge never issued, or one it has already consumed.
attacks.defended_by: Only a pending state this edge is still holding is accepted, and taking it consumes it.

attacks.what: A token signed by somebody else, or for somebody else, is presented as proof of identity.
attacks.defended_by: The ID token's signature is verified against the provider's JWKS and its claims against the provider that was asked.

attacks.what: The development identity stub, which signs anybody in as anybody, ships.
attacks.defended_by: It refuses to run unless a gate is set explicitly.

attacks.what: A caller reaches an entity's inbound API surface with no key, or with the wrong one.
attacks.defended_by: The key is compared in constant time before the handler runs at all.

attacks.what: A peer sends a frame large enough to be worth buffering, repeatedly.
attacks.defended_by: The frame cap rejects before buffering, and the read-buffer cap closes a connection whose peer outruns the reader.

attacks.what: One address opens connections until the edge runs out of something.
attacks.defended_by: Per-IP and global caps, applied inside the verifier.

attacks.what: A peer connects and never finishes the upgrade, holding a socket for free.
attacks.defended_by: A timer per pending upgrade closes it at security.handshake_timeout_ms.

attacks.what: Anything on the machine reaches the local design server's API and writes to the project.
attacks.defended_by: Every /api request carries a token minted for that run, compared in constant time.

attacks.what: A page the visitor is looking at resolves a name to 127.0.0.1 and drives the local design server as its own origin.
attacks.defended_by: The Host header has to be this server, and a request that says where it came from has to say this editor.

attacks.what: A signed-in visitor without the scope a member is gated on reads it anyway: the slot may refuse, but a prop and a model are pushed state and take no call to read.
attacks.defended_by: A `<scope>` gate is on the flow, not the shape. The Source answering that caller never seeds or follows a member they may not see, so no value is ever serialized toward them, and losing the scope withdraws what was already sent.

attacks.what: A signed-in visitor reaches the entity behind a front that serves a scope they do not hold, or an unauthorized caller reaches any of them.
attacks.defended_by: A front hands each caller to the entity its scope names and to no other, so no link to the rest is opened for them at all; the front's own member gate refuses a slot before anything is forwarded, so the entity behind never sees a call its caller had no scope for.

attacks.what: A genuine mesh entity that is not on a connect point's consumer list acquires it anyway.
attacks.defended_by: The consumer list is the whole of the rule: the owner refuses the connection at the point, so the Replica never becomes valid and the owner's QML needs no check of its own.

attacks.what: A browser console calls a slot the caller's scope does not reach, as in placeBid while signed out.
attacks.defended_by: The `<scope>` gate on the member is applied by the owner before the slot runs, so there is no check in the QML to forget.

attacks.what: A visitor is sent a login link whose `return` points somewhere the attacker controls, so the finished sign-in is redirected to them.
attacks.defended_by: The edge accepts one shape of return URL and no other: http, a loopback literal, a port, no userinfo, no path, no query, no fragment. Anything else refuses the login outright, before the provider is contacted.

attacks.what: Somebody reads the loopback URL back out of the system browser's history, or off a synced copy of it, and uses what it carried to sign in as that visitor.
attacks.defended_by: The URL carries a claim code, never the session. The code lives a minute, is spent by the first attempt whether or not that attempt was right, and buys nothing without the S256 verifier that never left the app.

attacks.what: A process on the same machine connects to the app's loopback port and hands it a claim code for an account the attacker controls, signing the visitor in as somebody else.
attacks.defended_by: The client refuses any arrival that does not carry the nonce it generated for the sign-in it started, compared in constant time, and claims nothing.

attacks.what: A loopback login is started against an edge whose project ships no desktop client, so the redirect goes to a port only something hostile would be listening on.
attacks.defended_by: The whole flow is off unless the project builds a desktop client: the login refuses the return, and the claim endpoint answers nothing.

attacks.what: Script on any page posts to the claim endpoint, spending a code a sign-in is halfway through.
attacks.defended_by: The endpoint refuses anything carrying an Origin at all, which puts it out of reach of page script rather than relying on the code being unguessable.

attacks.what: A device credential is copied off a disk and redeemed from another machine, alongside the machine it was taken from.
attacks.defended_by: Every redemption rotates, so the two copies diverge at the next relaunch. Presenting a retired generation past the overlap window revokes the family and every session it opened, which is what turns a silent theft into an event the edge acts on.

attacks.what: A device credential found on a disk is presented as the session cookie at the WebSocket upgrade.
attacks.defended_by: What is persisted is not a session. Neither half of it is a live session credential, so the upgrade verifier refuses it before a socket exists; it is only redeemable at one POST route, once.

attacks.what: Page script on any origin POSTs to the device route to turn a credential into a session in a browser.
attacks.defended_by: The route refuses any request carrying an Origin header at all, which puts it out of reach of page script rather than relying on the credential staying secret.

attacks.what: A visitor signs out, and the credential their app left on disk still buys a session.
attacks.defended_by: Signing out deletes the family the session came from, read from what the edge recorded when it minted that session rather than from anything the caller sent.

attacks.what: A visitor demoted since they signed in keeps the scope they had for the rest of their device credential's month.
attacks.defended_by: Redemption re-runs the scope mapping hook against the identity stored with the family, every time, instead of carrying a scope forward.

attacks.what: Somebody who learned a device family id offers wrong secrets for it to get its owner signed out.
attacks.defended_by: Only a retired generation past the overlap window revokes a family. A secret belonging to no generation is refused and costs the owner nothing, and the route is rate limited per address.

attacks.what: A machine whose secure store cannot complete a write signs its owner out: the rotation it could not save leaves the retired generation on disk, and the next launch presents it as a second copy in circulation.
attacks.defended_by: A write that fails, and a write abandoned at its deadline, both leave nothing behind, so the retired generation is never presented again and the family survives. Revocation stays the answer to two copies existing, which is what makes it worth acting on.

attacks.what: Somebody with read access to a machine's files copies the stored sign-in and replays it from their own, which a credential written to a file would let them do without ever facing the OS store that was supposed to protect it.
attacks.defended_by: There is no file fallback anywhere, on any platform or in any build: a machine with no secure store keeps the credential for the life of the process and signs in again next launch. Proved against the real config, data and cache directories rather than against the absence of a code path, with the store injected so the claim is checked on every platform and not only where a keyring happens to be missing.
